stem: What are the coordinates of the highest point on the graph?

figure.caption: Height of a Leaping Dolphin Above the Water
figure.alt: A downward-opening curve that starts on the horizontal axis at time 1, rises to a single highest point, and comes back down to the horizontal axis at time 5. The vertical axis is marked in steps of 4 feet.

explanation: The highest point is the vertex, where the curve turns around. It sits above 3 on the time axis. Follow it across to the vertical axis and it is level with 16, because that axis counts up in 4s (4, 8, 12, 16). So the vertex is $(3, 16)$. This is the reading step behind every 'maximum height' question: on the exam, once you have spotted the vertex, this is the whole job.

B.why: You read the right point but wrote the coordinates in the wrong order. A coordinate pair always gives the horizontal value first (time = 3), then the vertical value (height = 16).

C.why: You counted the gridlines up to the top of the curve (four of them) and wrote 4. The vertical axis goes up in 4s, so the fourth gridline stands for 16 feet.

D.why: $(5, 0)$ is where the dolphin goes back into the water, which is an x-intercept. You were asked for the highest point, the vertex.

stem: What is the $y$-intercept of the graph?

figure.caption: Elevation Along a Surveyed Map Route
figure.alt: An upward-opening curve that starts on the vertical axis, dips to a single lowest point, and rises again. The vertical axis is marked in steps of 2.

explanation: The $y$-intercept is where the graph crosses the vertical axis, which is where $x = 0$. Here the curve starts on the vertical axis level with 10, because that axis counts up in 2s (2, 4, 6, 8, 10). So the $y$-intercept is 10. This is what you are reading whenever the exam asks for a starting value, or for the value when the input is zero.

B.why: You counted gridlines (five of them) up to where the curve meets the axis and wrote 5. The vertical axis goes up in 2s, so the fifth gridline stands for 10.

C.why: 4 is how far along the horizontal axis the lowest point is, so it is the vertex's $x$-coordinate. The $y$-intercept is read on the vertical axis, at $x = 0$.

D.why: 2 is the height of the lowest point, which is the vertex's $y$-value. The $y$-intercept is where the curve meets the vertical axis, not where it bottoms out.

stem: What is the minimum value shown on the graph?

figure.caption: Price of a Bolt of Cotton Cloth in an 18th-Century Market
figure.alt: An upward-opening curve that starts high on the vertical axis, falls to a single lowest point, and rises back to the same height. The vertical axis is marked in steps of 5 shillings.

explanation: The minimum value is the height of the lowest point, the vertex. The curve bottoms out level with 10 on the vertical axis, which counts up in 5s (5, 10). So the minimum value is 10. Questions asking for the 'lowest price' or 'minimum cost' in words are asking for exactly this number.

B.why: 5 is where the lowest point sits on the horizontal axis (5 years after 1780). That tells you when the minimum happens, not what the minimum value is. A value is read on the vertical axis.

C.why: You counted gridlines up to the lowest point (two of them) and wrote 2. The vertical axis goes up in 5s, so the second gridline stands for 10.

D.why: 35 is the highest value on the graph, where the curve meets the vertical axis. You were asked for the lowest one.

stem: What are the coordinates of the $y$-intercept of the graph?

figure.caption: Air Temperature at a Weather Station
figure.alt: A downward-opening curve that starts on the vertical axis, rises to a single highest point, and falls back to the same height at the right edge. The vertical axis is marked in steps of 2 degrees.

explanation: The $y$-intercept is the point where the graph crosses the vertical axis, so its $x$-coordinate is 0. The curve meets that axis level with 10, because the axis counts up in 2s and 10 is the fifth gridline. So the point is $(0, 10)$. When an exam question asks for the $y$-intercept as a point, it wants this pair, and in a real-world setting it is the starting value.

B.why: You found the right values but swapped them. $(10, 0)$ would sit on the horizontal axis at 10 hours. The $y$-intercept always has $x = 0$, written first.

C.why: $(6, 28)$ is the highest point, the vertex. The $y$-intercept is where the curve meets the vertical axis, at $x = 0$.

D.why: You counted five gridlines up and wrote 5. The vertical axis goes up in 2s, so the fifth gridline stands for 10 degrees.
